Content:
Checking that the columns of [MATH: Q] form an orthonormal set is a fair amount of work. Thankfully, we have the following theorem to make our lives easier:

Content:
> A matrix [MATH: Q] is orthogonal if and only if
> [MATH: Q \cdot Q^T = Q^T \cdot Q = I]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: Q^T] denotes the transpose of [MATH: Q.] It's the matrix we get when we interchange the rows and columns of [MATH: Q.]
- To verify that a matrix is orthogonal in practice, we only need to check that [MATH: Q \, Q^T = I.]

[MATH: A \cdot A^T = A^T\cdot A = I] where [MATH: I] is the identity matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine the given statements.

  • Statement I is true. The number of rows in [MATH: A] is the same as the number of columns. So, it's a square matrix.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, [MATH: [(1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|(1)/(sqrt(2))]]

  • Statement III is true. Since [MATH: A\cdot A^T = I,] our matrix is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall the following theorem:

Content:
> A matrix [MATH: Q] is orthogonal if and only if
> [MATH: Q \cdot {\color{blue}{Q^T}} = {\color{blue}{Q^T}} \cdot Q = I.]

Content:
Now, recall that for [MATH: Q] to be invertible, there must exist a matrix [MATH: Q^{-1}] such that

Content:
[MATH: Q \cdot {\color{blue}{Q^{-1}}} = {\color{blue}{Q^{-1}}} \cdot Q = I.]

Content:
By comparing the two equations above, we can deduce the following:

Content:
- Every orthogonal matrix [MATH: Q] is invertible, and
- the inverse of an orthogonal matrix [MATH: Q] is [MATH: {\color{blue}{Q^T}},] that is
[MATH: Q^{-1} = Q^T.]

Content:
These properties explain why orthogonal matrices are desirable. We can always find the inverse of an orthogonal matrix, and we can quickly compute the inverse by simply transposing the original matrix.

2. [MATH: P^{-1}Q] is orthogonal
3. [MATH: PQ^T] is orthogonal

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that a matrix [MATH: Q] is orthogonal if and only if [MATH: Q Q^T = Q^T Q = I.]

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

  • For any orthogonal matrix [MATH: Q,] we have [MATH: Q^{-1} = Q^T.]

  • [MATH: (AB)^T = B^TA^T] for conformable matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B.]

With that in mind, let's inspect each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is false. Computing the product [MATH: 2Q \cdot (2Q)^T,] we obtain [MATH: 2Q ⋅ (2Q)^{T}|= 2Q ⋅ 2Q^{T}; = 4QQ^{T}; = 4I; ≠ I.]

  • Statement II is true. Computing the product [MATH: (P^{-1}Q)\cdot (P^{-1}Q)^T,] we obtain [MATH: (P^{− 1}Q) ⋅ (P^{− 1}Q)^{T}|= (P^{T}Q) ⋅ (P^{T}Q)^{T}; = P^{T}Q ⋅ Q^{T}(P^{T})^{T}; = P^{T}(QQ^{T})P; = P^{T}(I)P; = P^{T}P; = I.]

  • Statement III is true. Computing the product [MATH: (PQ^T)\cdot(PQ^T)^T ,] we obtain [MATH: (PQ^{T}) ⋅ (PQ^{T})^{T}|= PQ^{T} ⋅ (Q^{T})^{T}P^{T}; = PQ^{T}QP^{T}; = P(Q^{T}Q)P^{T}; = P(I)P^{T}; = PP^{T}; = I.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we have a square [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: Q] with columns [MATH: \mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_n{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [|||||; q_{1}|q_{2}|⋯|q_{n};|||||]]

Content:
The matrix [MATH: Q] is said to be orthogonal if its columns [MATH: \mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \dots, \mathbf{q}_n] form an orthonormal set. In other words,

Content:
- the columns of [MATH: Q] must be mutually orthogonal, and
- they must all be unit vectors.

Content:
For instance, the matrix
[MATH: [(sqrt(3))/(2)|− (1)/(2); (1)/(2)|(sqrt(3))/(2)]]
is orthogonal since its columns

Content:
[MATH: [(sqrt(3))/(2); (1)/(2)]]

Content:
form an orthonormal set [MATH: \left\{ {\color{black}\mathbf{q}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{q}_2} \right\}.] To see this, note the following:

Content:
- The vectors [MATH: \mathbf q_1] and [MATH: \mathbf q_2] are orthogonal, since
[MATH: q_{1} ⋅ q_{2}|= [(sqrt(3))/(2); (1)/(2)] ⋅ [− (1)/(2); (sqrt(3))/(2)]; = ((sqrt(3))/(2)) ⋅ (− (1)/(2)) + ((1)/(2)) ⋅ ((sqrt(3))/(2)); = − (sqrt(3))/(4) + (sqrt(3))/(4); = 0.]
- Both [MATH: \mathbf q_1] and [MATH: \mathbf q_2] are unit vectors, since
[MATH: ||q_{1}||^{2}|= q_{1} ⋅ q_{1}; = [(sqrt(3))/(2); (1)/(2)] ⋅ [(sqrt(3))/(2); (1)/(2)]; = ((sqrt(3))/(2))^{2} + ((1)/(2))^{2}; = (3)/(4) + (1)/(4); = 1,]
and
[MATH: ||q_{2}||^{2}|= q_{2} ⋅ q_{2}; = [− (1)/(2); (sqrt(3))/(2)] ⋅ [− (1)/(2); (sqrt(3))/(2)]; = (− (1)/(2))^{2} + ((sqrt(3))/(2))^{2}; = (1)/(4) + (3)/(4); = 1.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Straightforward Test of Orthogonality

Content:
Checking that the columns of [MATH: Q] form an orthonormal set is a fair amount of work. Thankfully, we have the following theorem to make our lives easier:

Content:
> A matrix [MATH: Q] is orthogonal if and only if
> [MATH: Q \cdot Q^T = Q^T \cdot Q = I]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- [MATH: Q^T] denotes the transpose of [MATH: Q.] It's the matrix we get when we interchange the rows and columns of [MATH: Q.]
- To verify that a matrix is orthogonal in practice, we only need to check that [MATH: Q \, Q^T = I.]

Content:
Let's see an example of applying this theorem.

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Orthogonal Matrices

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [(1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|(1)/(sqrt(2))]]

Consider the matrix [MATH: A] above. Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: A] is a square matrix
2. [MATH: A \cdot A^T = I]
3. [MATH: A] is an orthogonal matrix

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a square matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonal if and only if

[MATH: A \cdot A^T = A^T\cdot A = I]
where [MATH: I] is the identity matrix.

With that in mind, let's examine the given statements.

- Statement I is true. The number of rows in [MATH: A] is the same as the number of columns. So, it's a square matrix.
- Statement II is true. Indeed,
[MATH: [(1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|(1)/(sqrt(2))]]
- Statement III is true. Since [MATH: A\cdot A^T = I,] our matrix is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Inverse of an Orthogonal Matrix

Content:
Recall the following theorem:

Content:
> A matrix [MATH: Q] is orthogonal if and only if
> [MATH: Q \cdot {\color{blue}{Q^T}} = {\color{blue}{Q^T}} \cdot Q = I.]

Content:
Now, recall that for [MATH: Q] to be invertible, there must exist a matrix [MATH: Q^{-1}] such that

Content:
[MATH: Q \cdot {\color{blue}{Q^{-1}}} = {\color{blue}{Q^{-1}}} \cdot Q = I.]

Content:
By comparing the two equations above, we can deduce the following:

Content:
- Every orthogonal matrix [MATH: Q] is invertible, and
- the inverse of an orthogonal matrix [MATH: Q] is [MATH: {\color{blue}{Q^T}},] that is
[MATH: Q^{-1} = Q^T.]

Content:
These properties explain why orthogonal matrices are desirable. We can always find the inverse of an orthogonal matrix, and we can quickly compute the inverse by simply transposing the original matrix.

---

Item 7 — Example: Calculating the Inverse of an Orthogonal Matrix

Example Prompt:
Find the inverse of the orthogonal matrix [MATH: [(1)/(sqrt(2))|(1)/(sqrt(2)); − (1)/(sqrt(2))|(1)/(sqrt(2))]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The inverse of an orthogonal matrix is equal to its transpose.

Therefore, since [MATH: D] is orthogonal, we have

[MATH: D^{− 1}|= D^{T} = [(1)/(sqrt(2))|− (1)/(sqrt(2)); (1)/(sqrt(2))|(1)/(sqrt(2))].]

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: Properties of Orthogonal Matrices

Content:
Orthogonal matrices also have the following important properties:

Content:
- [MATH: \det(Q)=\pm1] (the determinant of an orthogonal matrix is either [MATH: 1] or [MATH: -1])
- If [MATH: \lambda] is an eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix [MATH: Q,] then [MATH: | \lambda |= 1 .]

Content:
Watch out! These properties are necessary but not sufficient conditions:

Content:
- Every orthogonal matrix has determinant equal to [MATH: \pm 1], but not every matrix with determinant [MATH: \pm 1] is orthogonal!
- Similarly, every orthogonal matrix has eigenvalues [MATH: 1] or [MATH: -1] only, but not every matrix with eigenvalues [MATH: 1] or [MATH: -1] is orthogonal.

---

Item 11 — Example: Calculating the Determinant of a Product of Matrices

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [(2)/(sqrt(13))|− (3)/(sqrt(13)); (3)/(sqrt(13))|(2)/(sqrt(13))]]

Find [MATH: |\textrm{det}(PQ)|] given that [MATH: P] is an orthogonal matrix.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We use the following facts:

- The determinant of a product is equal to the product of the determinants.
- The determinant of an orthogonal matrix [MATH: P] is equal to [MATH: \pm1.]

Applying these ideas, we get the following:

[MATH: |det(PQ)||=|det(P) ⋅ det(Q)|; =|(± 1) ⋅ det(Q)|; =|± 1|⋅|det(Q)|; =|det(Q)|; =|(− 2sqrt(3)) ⋅ 3sqrt(3) − 2 ⋅ 1|; =|− 18 − 2|; =|− 20|; = 20]
